newsitem.title: ITALY: Companies told to build cross-border brands.
newsitem.headline: Companies told to build cross-border brands.

text.p: International advertising experts said on Thursday companies had to build strong brands that could cross borders if they were to win turf in Europe's increasingly competitive consumer markets.

Ad agencies and multinational advertisers gathered at an industry conference in Rome said slow Western economic growth combined with a proliferation of products meant companies had to struggle to attract jaded consumers.

"Competition has become ferocious. Competitors move freely from country to country, into developed and developing economies alike," Peter Georgescu, chairman and chief executive officer of Young & Rubicam Inc, the U.S.-based advertising network, said.
He told the annual conference of the European Association of Advertising Agencies that big companies, in order to grow, had to make "cross-border marketing" a part of their strategy.
That meant having in-depth knowledge of consumer markets, a companies' own brands and what people thought of them.
John Englehart, Ogilvy & Mather's European client service director in London, said a key to winning and keeping marketshare was to distinguish one's brand from others.
"There has been a progressive shift from a battle of products to a battle of brands," he said.
He said O&M's top 10 clients, including International Business Machines Corp, American Express Co, Ford Motor Co, Unilever and Kraft General Foods all focused now on "cross-border marketing".
Englehart said the most successful cross-border marketing meant a company sent out a consistent message around the world, but tailored it, when necessary, to individual markets.
Russ Shaw, vice president for advertising and brand management at American Express, said tough global competition had prompted Amex to initiate a major corporate restructuring.

The reorganisation included re-evaluating the brand image of American Express and replacing a geographic management structure with one focused on either consumers, corporate cardholders or the stores that accept American Express.
He told delegates from ad agencies and trade bodies in 24 countries it was meant, among other things, to help American Express get new products out faster.
Shaw said 30 percent of American Express's "bottom line" now came from business outside the United States, and that was expected to grow to 50 percent by the year 2001.
Georgescu said Young & Rubicam had given clients competitive edge in new markets by spending time and money on a database that evaluated brand image and analysed markets.

He said the database divided people around the world into seven "psychographic" groups or mindsets: "mainstreamers", "succeeders", "resigned poor", "struggling poor", "transitionals", "reformers" and "aspirers".
